questions.q: What are the two financial statements where every adjustment must be reflected to complete the double entry?
questions.a: Every adjustment must be reflected in the Trading and Profit & Loss Account (or either Trading Account or Profit & Loss Account depending on the nature) and the Balance Sheet. A wrong answer (e.g., only in Profit & Loss Account) reveals the student has not grasped the dual aspect concept: adjustments simultaneously affect profit determination and financial position.

questions.q: Explain why closing stock is credited to the Trading Account but also shown on the asset side of the Balance Sheet.
questions.a: Closing stock is credited to Trading Account because it represents unsold goods that reduce the cost of goods sold (matching concept). It appears as a current asset in the Balance Sheet because it is an unsold resource owned by the business at year-end. A wrong answer (e.g., "it's income") shows confusion between revenue recognition and asset valuation.

questions.q: A Trial Balance shows Debtors ₹50,000, Bad Debts ₹2,000, and Provision for Doubtful Debts ₹1,500. Additional information: "Write off further bad debts ₹1,000 and maintain provision at 5% on debtors." Calculate the amount debited to Profit & Loss Account for provision for doubtful debts.
questions.a:
Step 1: Debtors after further bad debts = ₹50,000 - ₹1,000 = ₹49,000.
Step 2: New provision required = 5% of ₹49,000 = ₹2,450.
Step 3: Old provision = ₹1,500.
Step 4: Additional provision needed = ₹2,450 - ₹1,500 = ₹950 (debit to P&L).
A wrong answer (e.g., ₹2,450) reveals the student forgets to adjust for the existing provision balance.

questions.q: Compare the treatment of "Outstanding Expenses" and "Prepaid Expenses" in the Profit & Loss Account and Balance Sheet. How does each affect net profit?
questions.a: Outstanding expenses are added to the respective expense in P&L (increasing expense, decreasing profit) and shown as a current liability in Balance Sheet. Prepaid expenses are deducted from the respective expense in P&L (decreasing expense, increasing profit) and shown as a current asset in Balance Sheet. A wrong comparison (e.g., both increase profit) indicates the student hasn't internalized the accrual concept: expenses must match the period they belong to.

questions.q: A manager is entitled to 10% commission on net profit after charging such commission. The net profit before commission is ₹1,10,000. Evaluate whether the commission amount is ₹11,000 or ₹10,000 and justify.
questions.a: Commission is on profit AFTER commission, so formula: Commission = Profit before commission × Rate/(100+Rate) = ₹1,10,000 × 10/110 = ₹10,000. ₹11,000 would be correct only if commission were on profit BEFORE commission. Choosing ₹11,000 shows the student cannot distinguish between the two bases of commission calculation – a common board exam trap.

questions.q: Create a mini-case with a Trial Balance (5 accounts) and 3 adjustments that require the student to prepare a Trading Account, Profit & Loss Account, and Balance Sheet. Ensure one adjustment affects Trading Account, one affects Profit & Loss Account, and one affects both.
questions.a: Example: Trial Balance: Capital ₹1,00,000, Purchases ₹60,000, Sales ₹90,000, Wages ₹10,000, Furniture ₹20,000. Adjustments: (1) Closing Stock ₹15,000 (Trading), (2) Outstanding Wages ₹2,000 (Trading), (3) Depreciation on Furniture 10% (P&L and Balance Sheet). A poor answer would miss the dual effect of depreciation or misplace closing stock, showing inability to synthesize multiple adjustments.
